newsitem.title: UK: Salvesen shareholders voice anger over div.
newsitem.headline: Salvesen shareholders voice anger over div.

text.p: Gerald Elliot, former chairman of distribution and equipment hire group Christian Salvesen, said on Tuesday he was urging shareholders to vote against the board's plan to pay a special dividend.
He said the board's proposals should be rejected because he believed the dividend would seriously weaken the financial strength of the company.

Elliot, who says he has secured support from 14 percent of Christian Salvesen shareholders, also plans to bring in John Grant, formerly finance director of LucasVarity Plc, as chief executive if the board's proposals are defeated at a meeting on March 13.
"I believe that Salvesen's management has been performing badly for a number of years now and that changes at the top are required in the long term interests of shareholders," said Elliot.

Salvesen said last week it planned to pay a special dividend by way of a foreign income dividend, of 34 pence per share, totalling 100 million pounds. The dividend payout will be combined with a share capital consolidation.

In November last year the company announced that it would pay a special dividend of 150 million pounds and started the process this year when it paid an enhancement to the interim dividend of around 50 million pounds.
Shareholder approval is needed at the March 13 meeting to authorise the share capital and to increase Christian Salvesen's borrowing powers.
"I would regard such a defeat as a vote of no confidence in the two main architects of the board's proposals, namely the non-executive chairman and chief executive," said Elliot.
Newspapers have reported recently that concerns over tax liabilites are thought to be troubling many of the 400 Salvesen family members who control 37 percent of the company's shares.

Salvesen moved to silence critics in November with its plans for the special dividend payouts and proposals to demerge its Aggreko equipment hire business after the company rejected a 1.1 billion pounds hostile bid from Hays Plc.
Elliot, who has written to shareholders with his objections, also opposes the demerger which he says would expose the logistics business in a hostile market.
